rv.q: The result is an instant American classic: a tale of heartbreak and hardscrabble, poetic but not without fun in the guesthouse run by Nick and Elizabeth Laine.
Girl from the North Country is one of the most transporting shows I have seen in years.
A superb cast use Bob’s back catalogue to glorious effect in Conor McPherson’s astonishing cross-section of hope and stoic suffering in Depression-era Minnesota.
The idea is inspired and the treatment piercingly beautiful.
In the end, the power of the music wins out and the show sends you out on a high, with Dylan's lyrics embedded in your head, destined to stay there for days.
It's a mood piece, marrying the myths of Dylan and the Depression into something timeless and elegant – a stark evocation of the American firmament.
It also yawns between the thrill of this production when it sings and its perversely melodramatic flatness when it’s behaving like a traditional play.
I have to confess to being a mite underwhelmed by this valiant and undeniably accomplished effort to do something more oblique and intriguing with songs that will outlive us all.
I'm glad I didn't listen to them and checked it out for myself because I thought it exceptional.

These songs seem to come at us as new, thrilling discoveries of powerful secrets about the human condition, perfectly given form and shape and textures of voice and instrumentation that will have them ringing on and on in your mind long after you leave the theatre.
The blend slips down easy: enjoyable and soulful.
The result is a show of great poetry with a haunting intensity that stays with the audience.
Theatrical experiences as magical as this are rare, see it while you can.

Dylan’s 1960s and 1970s protest songs are remarkably pertinent to the more desperate social conditions of 30 or 40 years before. McPherson uses them with great originality as a distillation of communal experience. McPherson also draws excellent work from his entire cast.
For all its rough edges, I loved it.

cn.t: Critics praise McPherson's sophisticated fusion of Dylan's songbook with Depression-era storytelling as "pure genius" and "theatrical magic." The inventive production earns acclaim for its haunting arrangements and superb cast.
